column3: Immediately after the fire, all routines collapsed. The participant moved in with a sibling and spent the first two weeks focused almost entirely on understanding insurance and stabilizing basic needs. Early use of United Policyholders and disaster recovery centers was highly effective because they provided centralized guidance and pointed the participant toward the right next steps. The second phase shifted into replacing essentials and securing medium-term housing. Finding pet-friendly housing was a major practical barrier; the participant was fortunate to secure a furnished rental close to work, but noted that many others struggled significantly with pet accommodations. Insurance through Allstate was unusually smooth and fast, reimbursing receipts quickly and covering full rebuild limits plus extended coverage. This financial stability reduced substantial stress. The participant identified the hardest part not as finances, but being abruptly disconnected from established routines and normal life structures.
column4: Emotional recovery improved over time, but grief remained persistent and specific. The participant described difficulty with the loss of home as a symbolic and emotional anchor—something as simple as saying “I’m going home” became painful because home no longer existed. The loss of family heirlooms, genealogical archives, and inherited furniture carried profound grief, especially because the participant viewed themselves as the keeper of family history. Intrusive imagery of cherished objects burning remained vivid. Emotional regulation was supported by daily dog walks, regular peer connection with friends (many of whom were also affected), and community volunteering through Habitat for Humanity, which restored connection and purpose. Financial reassurance from insurance payouts significantly reduced existential anxiety, including uncertainty about retirement. Physical progress in rebuilding (debris clearing, foundation laid, framing preparation) restored hope by making recovery tangible. Community rituals, such as ceremonies hosted by a local Jewish synagogue, also provided emotional grounding and communal healing.
column5: The biggest early decision was whether to rebuild or relocate, and making that decision was difficult due to emotional overload. Once rebuilding was chosen, permitting became the major burden. The participant struggled to understand county processes, architectural timelines, and technical requirements—especially because their property included a septic system, adding complexity. Even experienced architects and builders were uncertain about submission requirements because they were early in the recovery wave. Errors and omissions in submitted plans delayed progress. Housing relocation was also highly competitive and stressful, with many survivors competing for limited rentals and stories of exploitative rents or deposit disputes. The participant noted that stronger housing navigation support would have been helpful. While insurance was not a pain point in this case, the participant acknowledged that insurance reform and housing support systems remain major systemic issues for others.
column6: Now retired, the participant has more time to manage the rebuild, but described it as essentially another full-time job. Ongoing needs center around decision-making, contractor management, rebuilding oversight, and maintaining momentum over a long timeline.
column7: Insurance tools (receipt-tracking apps) and self-built spreadsheets helped manage reimbursement and track spending. Community survivor groups such as the Eaton Fire Survivors Network (EFSN) provided spreadsheets and organizational tools, though some felt overly complex for this participant’s needs. Content inventory was a major challenge; tools and templates from United Policyholders were especially helpful because they simplified household inventory reconstruction. Digital community tools (e.g., Discord, Zoom meetings) were valuable for staying informed about policyholder issues and insurance reform. The participant highlighted inventorying losses as one of the most emotionally difficult and administratively heavy tasks and strongly endorsed tools that could reduce both the emotional and cognitive burden.
column8: The participant saw clear utility for AI in two practical areas: (1) contents inventory and (2) insurance policy interpretation. They expressed strong interest in uploading an insurance policy into AI to receive plain-language summaries and ask clarifying questions about coverage categories (e.g., buildings vs exterior structures). AI was viewed as a strong cognitive support tool for reducing confusion and increasing clarity. However, for emotional support (e.g., meditation), the participant preferred human connection over AI, believing emotional processing is more meaningful in relationship with others.  Participant emphasized the need for highly practical, step-by-step procedural guidance, especially for permitting systems (e.g., EPIC-LA), document review, and contractor vetting. They wanted tools that could walk them through submissions, identify missing paperwork, review architectural plans for errors, and help evaluate contractors (licenses, interview questions, fit).
column9: procedural scaffolding reduces distress. This participant was relatively well-resourced and well-insured, yet still struggled heavily with permitting, inventorying, and contractor navigation. Even when money is not the bottleneck, process complexity is.

column3: The participant’s recovery rapidly transformed into large-scale community activism rather than personal recovery. As co-founder of Eaton Fire Survivors United, the participant became deeply involved in organizing contamination testing, building what they describe as the largest wildfire contamination dataset in the nation, collaborating with scientists from Jet Propulsion Laboratory, University of California, Los Angeles, and other institutions. This activism emerged after direct institutional failures: when seeking soil testing guidance from Federal Emergency Management Agency and United States Environmental Protection Agency, they found no clear protocols or support. In response, they created community-driven systems to fill those gaps. The participant is now drafting legislation to establish standards for post-fire chemical contamination testing and advocating against competing legislation they believe minimizes harm in “standing homes” (homes still structurally standing but chemically contaminated). Personal recovery has been deliberately slowed in favor of systems-level advocacy. The participant’s background in activism, civic leadership, entertainment, and prior caregiving for a seriously ill parent positioned them to move quickly into organizer mode. Their mother’s earlier illness had already required deep healthcare navigation before the fire.
column4: Emotional processing appears heavily displaced into action. The participant explicitly described not pausing to process, instead moving immediately from one task to the next. Activism functions as both coping mechanism and mission. The daily reality is described as relentless (“a firehose”) with hundreds of emails per day and constant demands, suggesting chronic activation and sustained cognitive/emotional overload.
column5: While not directly elaborated in this section, the interview strongly implies that institutional ambiguity and the lack of contamination standards for standing homes are the central pain points. Insurance delays and lack of remediation support continue to obstruct personal recovery. The participant views current systems as structurally failing survivors with contamination-related losses, creating both practical and political burdens.
column6: No explicit standalone responses provided. Implicitly, ongoing needs include balancing activism with personal recovery, slowing down enough to process loss, and eventually remediating and returning home safely.

column22: Trying to navigate how we we return home when there is so much contamination in the soil that is going unaddressed by the federal and state governments. Furthermore insurance is forcing people back into contaminated homes by claiming their homes can be cleaned of wildfire debris but the contamination remains, EFRU, a resident led data driven organization holding the most data on WUI impacted standing homes in the nation, reports 96% of homes still have lead and 36% of homes still have asbestos after remediation. Insurance companies are ending ALE and effectively forcing people back into contaminated homes because they have nowhere else to live. Currently there are no regulations on thresholds for contamination in standing homes caused by a WUI, so insurance companies claim they're not responsible for removing the contamination caused by smoke and ash in people's homes which includes asbestos, lead, arsenic, chromium, thallium, beryllium, lithium, and more. People are having to choose between being financially ruined or their health. 7 out of 10 residents remain displaced according to Dept of Angels. You can learn more about the contamination found in the wildfire that infiltrated residents' homes by going to www.efru.la.

If there were standards for indoor contamination for asbestos dust, lead dust, and all the other CAM-17 metals, if insurance companies didn't try to overturn independent industrial hygienist tests by sending in their own contractors who report much less contamination impact (but don't test HVACs, behind walls, or attics), and if the state and the federal government actually provided funds and a systematic approach to soil remediation, thousands of us with standing homes could be home by now. We all face exposing ourselves to extremely high contamination levels, but there are no protections for us currently. AB 1642 provides some protections from contamination if it passes. 
 

 Learn more by going to www.EFRU.LA.

column3: The participant experienced a layered disruption: smoke damage (not full burn), insurance conflict, and career loss. The smoke-damaged home created a more ambiguous and prolonged recovery than a total loss, which the participant described as harder in many ways. Initially took a month off work, but once returning to work at Jet Propulsion Laboratory, the insurance battle functioned like a second full-time job, especially because adjusters only worked during business hours and could not be compartmentalized around employment. This led to reducing work hours to part-time, followed by eventual layoff. The layoff created an existential rupture and forced career reinvention, with plans to start a business. Even more than a year later, about half of the participant’s time is still spent on insurance and recovery-related tasks. The acute aftermath was chaotic: scattered resources, unstable access, lack of centralized information, and logistical overwhelm. Social media (especially Facebook groups) became a primary survival tool for locating aid, supplies, and updated information. Housing placement was another major issue—insurance-provided options were geographically impractical, and proximity to home/community was identified as crucial for recovery.
column4: The participant framed the experience as a form of moral injury, not just trauma. The emotional burden was compounded by witnessing systemic failures: disabled neighbors died after calling 911 and not receiving help, looting occurred without adequate response, and broader climate-driven injustice shaped the participant’s interpretation of the event. The participant described the disaster as layered and existential—an injustice rather than random misfortune. There was also emotional dissonance around survival: initially feeling lucky the house survived, then later recognizing that contamination may have created a worse long-term burden than total loss. Watching neighbors rebuild quickly while remaining trapped in contamination and insurance limbo intensified feelings of inequity and stuckness.
column5: The participant strongly emphasized the need for a case manager or dedicated navigator—someone to offload the cognitive and logistical burden and provide structured, trustworthy guidance. Friends offered support, but generic support was less useful than task-specific help. The participant even explored hiring assistants because the mental load was so high. The central pain point was not just volume of tasks but the burden of sequencing, tracking, and decision-making under stress.
column6: The dominant ongoing need is inventorying and documenting contaminated belongings for insurance and legal purposes. Because the home is contaminated, nearly everything (except pure glass or metal) must be cleaned, documented, or discarded with precision. This requires a highly detailed inventory (already over 1,000 items), often with exact product-level documentation rather than generic descriptions. The process has consumed hundreds of hours. Physically re-entering the contaminated home—even with full PPE—causes illness, forcing limited exposure and slowing progress. The participant feels trapped because only they can complete this documentation, and it is necessary for litigation.
column7: Technology is central to the participant’s recovery infrastructure. They maintain a highly organized Google Google Drive repository of documentation, contractor quotes, contamination reports, and insurance paperwork. Large language models were used for inventory support (e.g., generating lists from photographs of shelves, refrigerators, and pantries), which helped but still required substantial manual correction. Social media, especially Facebook groups and Discord, were described as irreplaceable because they surface real-time, situationally relevant information. However, AI tools like ChatGPT were mixed—sometimes useful, but sometimes inaccurate or fabricated regulatory guidance, requiring verification.
column8: No explicit direct attitudinal statements were provided, but usage patterns suggest cautious pragmatism: AI is useful for administrative acceleration and pattern extraction, but cannot be trusted without verification. Accuracy is essential because mistakes in legal or insurance contexts carry real consequences.
column9: contamination recovery is a different disaster category. It creates legal, physical, cognitive, and emotional burdens distinct from total loss. TAC may need separate workflows for smoke/chemical contamination survivors, not just a “house damaged” category.

column32: Inventory. And there isn't a spot for this but I want to share a hesitancy with an AI tool for recovery. Through this process we have all become experts and our situations are nuanced. Each person's recovery is different, which is what makes resources difficult in general; of course they need to be designed for the "average" but in recovery there is so much variation and nuance and specificity. I would have a hard time trusting an AI tool right now because we have been pathfinding our way through this recovery and I only really trust information that I have personally experienced or verified. It's too risky to assume that AI is providing the right answer to something.

column34: Say yes to help and accept it all when it floods in the beginning, especially financial. It stops after a while and you'll need it. If you know you or your neighbors were in the middle of the disaster, just sign a 1-year lease on an temporary living situation (with understanding of the fee for breaking the lease). If you don't need to be displaced for a year, great! You can break your lease and move home. But most likely you'll need it, and you will save yourself a significant amount of stress by having a stable living situation.

column3: Hasn’t changed a lot structurally—we’re just living in a different place close to home. Miss the house, yard, and community. Day-to-day setting has changed a lot, but we’ve adapted and are making the best of it. The rebuild process is a lot: insurance payments, inspections, SBA loan navigation, getting funds in hand to keep rebuilding moving. Responsibilities are shared organically between partners. For another participant, day-to-day routines and support systems stayed mostly the same, with charitable organizations providing generous support and architects/contractors becoming new parts of life. Another reflected that the first month felt extremely hard, and that early access to a “crash course” on rebuilding, contractors, and process navigation would have reduced confusion and accelerated progress. Peer support groups and architect connections became especially helpful.
column4: The emotional aftermath involved desperation, uncertainty, anxiety, and major questions about whether rebuilding was possible and financially feasible. Stability—especially securing a place to stay quickly and re-establishing routines—was one of the most protective factors. Working as a team with a spouse was described as critical for emotional coping and navigating recovery. Charitable support and prior preparedness helped reduce distress and offered reassurance.
column5: Financial recovery was the biggest pain point—figuring out how to get back to what life was before. There was a strong focus on moving forward and avoiding getting emotionally stuck. Participants highlighted the value of practical education about rebuilding (a “crash course”) and noted that while therapy and community support were available, those resources were not always personally appealing or relevant. For some, returning to work provided structure and distraction.
column6: The primary ongoing need is getting back home through rebuilding. Progress is tied directly to accessing and releasing insurance funds from escrow. There were no major evolving emotional or practical needs identified beyond moving the rebuild process forward.
column7: Basic internet searches were the main technology used for navigating recovery, particularly for understanding insurance, maximizing benefits, and locating charitable resources.
column8: AI was viewed with skepticism. Participant reported trying AI tools but finding them only marginally useful, mainly for narrowing information rather than offering transformative help. Another participant emphasized that if AI were used in recovery, tone matters: it should feel soothing, calming, and emotionally attuned rather than robotic.

column3: Life changed dramatically after the fire, though a sense of normalcy slowly returns over time. The transition from immediate survival mode back into everyday life happens gradually and almost imperceptibly. Immediate displacement involved staying with family, then hotels, while continuing major life milestones (e.g., son’s senior year and theatre auditions) under disrupted conditions. Practical tools like keeping a notebook for case numbers and tasks were essential for tracking recovery. Accessing emergency aid (clothing, FEMA funds) helped stabilize things early. Insurance was a major stressor—participants felt underinsured and unprepared for the complexity of navigating claims, often perceiving insurance companies as adversarial and requiring constant self-advocacy. Recovery felt like managing a full-time and part-time job simultaneously, including emotionally exhausting inventorying of lost possessions. Grief emerged incrementally over time, especially around sentimental losses (books, toys, family traditions). Social media (Instagram, Facebook, Discord) became critical information hubs, and practical advice from community members (e.g., retired adjusters) was highly valuable. Relationships were strained by uncertainty and fear, but dividing responsibilities helped. Family members grieved differently, requiring patience and emotional space.
column4: Recovery is emotionally exhausting and deeply tied to practical burdens. The constant stream of applications (SBA loans, mortgage relief, aid programs) created fatigue and decision overload. Having a partner was described as essential for sharing burdens and maintaining hope when one person felt depleted. Rebuilding progress (65% complete) offered visible hope and motivation, especially when physically seeing the home take shape again. Trusted community referrals (builders, agents, neighbors) reduced uncertainty and emotional strain. Social connectedness—through neighborhood text chains and shared rebuilding efforts—provided reassurance and collective hope.
column5: The biggest challenge was fragmentation of information and support. Resources existed, but survivors lacked centralized, streamlined guidance on how to access them or in what order (FEMA, insurance, adjusters, mental health, rebuilding). There was frustration with institutional processes and a desire for less bureaucracy and more empathy. Survivors emphasized that older adults or those with less technological literacy would need much more hands-on human support. Mental health resources would be especially important for those without prior therapy access. Public adjusters were described as useful but expensive, often taking 20–25% of settlements, highlighting the tradeoff between reducing stress and losing substantial funds.
column6: No direct responses provided. Implicitly, needs evolved from immediate survival (housing, clothing, paperwork) to long-term rebuilding, insurance negotiation, and emotional processing of cumulative losses over time
column7: AI became a practical advocacy tool in disputes with insurance and mortgage companies. Participants used AI to analyze adjuster reports, identify missing items or code compliance issues, and draft dispute reports using California building codes and “good faith” insurance standards. AI was also used to identify relevant politicians, agencies, and senators to strengthen advocacy efforts. A key benefit was helping generate fact-based, non-emotional language during high-conflict negotiations with insurers. This transformed AI from an information tool into an advocacy amplifier.
column8: No explicit attitudinal reflections on AI were provided, but usage patterns suggest AI was perceived as highly valuable when it improved leverage, precision, and advocacy in bureaucratic disputes. It was used strategically rather than emotionally.
column9: information asymmetry is the stress multiplier. The distress isn’t just from loss—it’s from being forced into adversarial systems (insurance, aid, rebuild) without a map.

column3: Participant’s house was the “last house standing” but remained uninhabitable due to toxin contamination, creating a uniquely difficult recovery path. There was no evacuation notice initially, leading to multiple emergency relocations. The participant lived with friends for months before securing longer-term housing. Insurance delays and reversals created significant instability, forcing legal action. Recovery became a daily cognitive and logistical burden, requiring at least two hours a day managing lawyers, SBA, insurance, and rebuilding coordination. Extended family losses compounded the disruption, with multiple relatives losing homes and schools. Parenting during recovery added complexity, with children processing trauma very differently—one child withdrawing and another seeking repeated exposure and discussion to make sense of the event. Social support systems (friends, survivor networks, therapists) became essential, deepening relationships and providing practical and emotional scaffolding. Participant received a PTSD diagnosis and engaged in therapy.
column4: The emotional burden was strongly linked to legal and practical advocacy. Having attorneys the participant trusted created relief and containment, reducing the psychological burden of fighting insurance and utility companies alone. Trustworthy advocates created emotional stabilization in an otherwise adversarial process.
column5: The participant described a major gap in disaster systems for survivors with “standing structures” (homes not destroyed but contaminated). Existing disaster systems, policies, and public discourse centered on total-loss cases, leaving this group overlooked and underserved. Insurance pushed the participant to re-enter an unsafe home despite no utilities and contamination risks. The participant noted that in some ways total loss would have been easier because pathways for recovery were clearer. This “partial loss” or contamination-only category created ambiguity, neglect, and additional stress.
column6: Participant used AI by uploading their insurance policy into OpenAI’s ChatGPT to ask clarifying questions and better understand policy language. They identified project management as an unmet need—keeping all recovery tasks mentally organized was overwhelming. A personal assistant or structured task management system would have significantly reduced burden.
column7: No formal technology tools beyond AI policy review were described, but the participant relied heavily on social media survivor networks (especially the Eaton Fire Survivor Network) for real-time information about grants, aid, and contractors. Peer-based digital communities were among the most useful recovery tools
column8: AI was viewed as a powerful research and organizational tool but potentially risky for emotionally vulnerable people. The participant emphasized that AI is “a tool, not a real thing,” and worried some survivors might over-attach or over-trust it during vulnerability. They saw strong value in AI as an executive functioning aid: timeline reminders (FEMA, SBA, grants, sleep check-ins), application deadlines, recovery milestones, and tailored grant matching. The participant also highlighted the value of AI-assisted inventory tools (e.g., photo-based valuation systems) for documenting losses. The strongest use case for AI was as an executive functioning coach and organizational assistant rather than emotional replacement.
column9: partial-loss survivors are a blind spot. Most recovery systems appear designed for binary categories (home gone vs. home intact), but contamination cases create a third category with major ambiguity.

column33: Don't expect your insurance company to be your advocate, even though you have paid for the coverage. They immediately become your adversary because they don't care about you personally. column34: First, take a breath and know that recovery is likely to take longer than you imagine. Pay attention to the people who step up and support you. Lean on them, even if it's friends instead of family. Prepare for emotions to hit at unexpected times and allow them to come. Give yourself grace, space, and time. Lots of all of them.

column3: Recovery was described as highly disruptive and chaotic, especially in the first 3–4 months, with confusion about what needed to happen next. Being a full-time student added another layer of complexity, requiring accommodations from instructors while pushing through coursework during acute recovery. Housing instability was a major disruption—moving between hotels and family homes before eventually renting a house and re-establishing some routine. FEMA hotel navigation was cumbersome and labor-intensive, requiring multiple calls and self-advocacy. Insurance was described more positively than in other interviews, with upfront payments and housing support, though inventorying losses remained difficult, especially for inherited or irreplaceable items without receipts. The participant used therapeutic strategies to narrow focus to immediate needs (“what do I need right now?”), which helped manage overwhelm. Family support, long-standing therapy, social networks, and practical community resources were critical. Executive functioning impairment was a major issue, and centralized information about aid and recovery resources was identified as a major unmet need. Psychological First Aid and anticipatory guidance (what to expect at 3, 6, 12 months) were seen as highly valuable.
column4: Emotional stabilization took time and included pharmacological support (Lexapro) to regulate mood and improve functioning. At six months, the participant felt more distance from the trauma and began integrating the loss. Mourning was ongoing but more manageable. Practical recovery tasks (e.g., contractors, rebuilding) were initially too overwhelming, requiring partner support. Re-engaging with the property and seeing undamaged parts of the yard recover created hope and served as a symbol of personal recovery and resilience.
column5: Information overload and fragmentation were major barriers. Participants used ChatGPT and Claude to help with practical recovery tasks like insurance inventory language, purchasing decisions, and resource finding. Social media and trusted local voices became essential informal hubs for centralized information. Community networks (e.g., WeChat groups) were highly valuable for sharing real-time practical information (permits, propane, RV living logistics). column3: Life changed immediately upon learning of the loss. The first 8–12 weeks were dominated by immediate survival and stabilization tasks: insurance, rehousing, replacing essentials like clothes and toiletries, and pausing normal work and personal commitments. Extended family support (especially cousins) was critical in the acute phase, providing housing and practical assistance. The participant took on a caregiver role for parents, especially helping navigate technology, online systems, and long-term planning. Trauma significantly impaired the parents’ ability to make decisions or plan for the future. Complicating recovery, the participant’s mother was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease three weeks after the fire, increasing cognitive and emotional burden and further complicating decision-making. The participant’s own support system (spouse, parent community) helped buffer the caregiving load, including practical support for their daughter. Tension later emerged when the parents questioned the participant’s decisions and support efforts, which created emotional pain and distance.
column4: The participant primarily operated in “doer mode,” suppressing their own emotional needs while focusing on caregiving and logistics. Early on, parents accepted support, which made caregiving feel effective and purposeful. Over time, as family dynamics shifted and support became questioned, the participant experienced hurt and emotional withdrawal. There was a strong sense of abandonment by the broader public—initial support and concern faded quickly, especially once other political and societal events took over attention. This fading of collective attention was painful for the parents. One major emotional turning point was the parents purchasing a new home in Altadena, returning to familiar streets and routines, which significantly improved their mental state. The participant learned that stepping back and only providing support when invited reduced conflict and preserved the relationship.
column5: Insurance, expected to be the biggest stressor, turned out to be relatively smooth and fast, which was a positive surprise. Government disaster fairs that consolidated services (federal and state support for replacing IDs, passports, etc.) were highly effective and reduced friction. The emotional burden, however, remained the most difficult aspect—especially for the participant as a secondary survivor/caregiver. There was pressure to contain their own grief because the parents were already emotionally overwhelmed. A major gap identified was finding emotionally acceptable pathways for older adults to engage with therapy or support, especially when stigma exists. Integrating emotional support into practical service touchpoints (e.g., document replacement, clothing drives, community gathering spaces) was suggested as a more organic way to normalize support-seeking.
column6: No explicit standalone entries, but needs evolved from immediate stabilization and logistics to longer-term caregiving, emotional support, financial planning, and adjusting family boundaries as parents regained agency.

Peer-based survivor networks (including connections to survivors from Healdsburg wildfires) provided structured checklists and step-by-step recovery roadmaps, which were especially valuable because they broke recovery into manageable weekly tasks. Legislative changes in California since earlier wildfire events were noted as improving the recovery process for newer survivors.

There was concern about generational misunderstanding of AI, particularly among older adults who associate it with job loss or social disruption. The biggest concern was misinformation. AI was seen as potentially useful for caregivers as well, but within limits: the participant emphasized the importance of helping only as much as survivors want to be helped and protecting the caregiver’s own time and boundaries.

column3: Participant had lived in Pacific Palisades since 1997 and experienced the fire as surreal and catastrophic, “like being in a movie.” Initial denial gave way to evacuation, including returning to retrieve forgotten items under dangerous conditions. The family was displaced for three months. The disruption was both emotional and logistical: navigating smoke damage, invisible toxins, insurance, and federal systems became a full-time job, replacing the participant’s planned retirement. Both adult children also lost homes, creating multigenerational recovery strain. The participant’s daughter was able to relocate with more financial stability, while the son, who had also lost employment alongside his spouse, was forced to sell his home and move into a rental due to unsustainable mortgage costs. The participant emphasized that the community became the strongest source of support—sharing practical recovery information, insurance strategies, and emotional solidarity. A major challenge was deciding whether to return to the home amid uncertainty about toxins and long-term health risks. Ultimately, age and life stage influenced the decision to stay and rebuild rather than relocate.
column4: The fire experience felt apocalyptic and destabilizing, with images of police and National Guard making it feel like “a bomb had fallen.” Returning to normal community life became a major source of hope and healing. Re-establishing access to familiar systems (e.g., transferring prescriptions back home, seeing neighborhood rebuilding, reopening community centers and stores) created emotional relief and optimism. The reopening of social spaces and reconnecting with familiar people (neighbors, pharmacists) carried strong emotional significance, with some community members openly crying upon reunion. These rituals of return helped rebuild belonging and hope.
column5: The biggest challenges centered on uncertainty: invisible toxins, unclear health implications, and distrust in testing processes. The participant questioned the reliability of government reports and insurance-funded environmental assessments, perceiving financial incentives for minimization of damage. Insurance advocacy required substantial self-education and persistence, including learning what was actually covered (e.g., HVAC systems, mattresses, fabrics, interior and exterior painting). There was strong frustration about the absence of centralized information and clear step-by-step guidance. Even with community meetings, the volume of information remained overwhelming. Participants described anger and distrust about how recovery funds were distributed and perceived government failures at local and federal levels. Empowerment through education and clearer guidance around toxicology, rebuilding decisions, and insurance negotiations was identified as critical.
column6: Participant attempted to engage in a neighborhood “block captain” program to support recovery efforts and stay involved but never received a response. This created frustration and a sense of being lost in the system. Over time, there was a growing need for meaningful participation, agency, and inclusion in community recovery efforts—not just passive receipt of information.
column7: Technology was used primarily for fast information gathering. The participant relied on internet searches and AI tools to quickly understand complex issues and policy questions (e.g., urban density planning versus evacuation logistics). Speed and efficiency of information retrieval were key benefits.
column8: AI was viewed positively as an information tool, especially for rapidly surfacing pros/cons and practical guidance. The participant’s husband, a psychiatrist, also used AI to support patient education around emotions and medications, suggesting a degree of professional trust in the technology. However, the participant strongly differentiated informational AI from emotional care: AI could help people explore issues (relationships, identity, emotional struggles), but deeper mental health processing still requires human connection. There was concern about isolation and over-reliance on AI for emotional work. For practical recovery tasks (e.g., toxicity testing disputes, insurance issues), AI could be highly useful if it offered deeper, more sophisticated assistance beyond repetitive or superficial responses.

column3: The first phase after the fire involved immediate displacement and instability, followed by a prolonged transitional period of house-sitting, apartment living, and rebuilding basic life infrastructure from scratch (furniture, clothing, household essentials). Early recovery involved trying to establish normalcy while simultaneously managing increasingly intense insurance demands and financial logistics. For 3–4 months, life felt “three times full,” with ordinary responsibilities layered on top of disaster recovery. Even after stabilization, the long-term horizon of rebuilding (estimated at 3 years, embedded in an 8–10 year life plan) creates an ongoing chronic burden. Community routines became an important stabilizer, and participation in an active neighborhood block captain program (weekly Zoom calls with 20–55 people) created ongoing social support and a reliable channel for information. A major unmet need was consistent, centralized guidance about insurance, permits, contractor selection, and rebuilding options. Participants noted that even a year later they were still discovering critical information they should have known earlier. A major burden was the need to constantly double- and triple-check information across multiple sources, including city agencies and insurers, because trust was low and guidance was inconsistent. Insurance interactions were especially difficult because they lacked trauma-informed communication and required repetitive retelling of the recovery timeline.
column4: The participant described the experience as “akin to PTSD” and moved through phases of resistance, immersion, execution, and delayed emotional processing. The emotional impact lagged behind the practical response. One of the participant’s coping strategies was transforming the experience into service—using their work to help others and later speaking publicly about resilience. This helped create meaning, momentum, and internal processing. Therapy and counseling were important supports. Family dynamics were complex: one child who remained local felt the emotional burden deeply, while other children were more emotionally distant from the experience. The participant also observed the indirect emotional effects on children who did not lose homes themselves but were deeply affected by watching parents and community suffer.
column5: The biggest pain points were uncertainty and the financial cost of recovery. There was significant ambiguity about whether and how the community would “return,” and a sense that even if it did, it would not be the same. Loss of control over key outcomes was distressing. The participant advocated for a formal resilience hub—an organized, expert-driven structure that could rapidly mobilize knowledge, coordinate resources, and serve as a centralized decision-support system for disaster survivors. This would reduce fragmentation and confusion.
column6: No direct standalone entries, but ongoing needs include long-term planning support, coordinated information management, emotional processing, and system navigation over multiple years rather than months.
column7: Communication platforms like Slack and WhatsApp were used heavily, but the sheer volume of messages became overwhelming and difficult to follow, making it hard to extract actionable information. There was no unified digital tool for recovery because each domain (insurance, rebuilding, permits, utilities) operated independently with separate systems and timelines. Even city agencies working on the same recovery process were poorly coordinated. Mental health support from Didi Hirsch Mental Health Services was described as highly valuable and process-oriented.

AI was seen as valuable for administrative and procedural work (e.g., permitting), freeing humans to focus on more complex or relational work. For emotional support, the participant was open to AI-assisted self-regulation (e.g., meditation, reflection), but emphasized that emotional needs are highly personal and relational. Human touch, especially through spouses and community, remains irreplaceable.

column3: Disaster recovery became a “second job” layered on top of full-time professional work, with very few weekends untouched by recovery-related tasks. Early on, the burden was dominated by insurance, rebuilding decisions, and logistical management. Even as acute demands lessened, the recovery workload remained persistent and chronic. The participant described oscillating between collapse (“completely broken down”) and hyper-functioning survival mode (“amped up”), with survival mode dominating in the early phase. Because they were often ahead of others in problem-solving, offers of help were sometimes shut down because they weren’t targeted or useful. The participant noted that having a concrete list of actionable tasks for helpers would have made accepting support easier. Practical social support (e.g., a friend setting up a GoFundMe fundraiser) filled critical gaps that the participant didn’t have bandwidth to manage.
column4: The participant became highly selective about social contact, cutting off people who were not directly helpful due to limited emotional bandwidth. This created isolation, and they noticed emotional rupture when confronted with “normal” life continuing around them (e.g., hearing a family laughing while they were immersed in crisis). The participant described difficulty tolerating others’ emotional distance from the disaster. There was also frustration and envy when comparing recovery experiences with neighbors whose losses were structurally different (e.g., smoke damage vs. full loss), though over time the participant recognized that partial-loss cases could be equally or more difficult. Emotional regulation improved once strategic priorities were clarified and recovery goals were stack-ranked (insurance vs. rebuilding), reducing decision chaos. Making clear strategic choices created emotional relief and momentum.
column5: The biggest challenge was not lack of information but lack of relevant information. Recovery pathways varied dramatically depending on the survivor’s specific situation (owner vs renter, full loss vs smoke damage, etc.), making generic advice largely unhelpful. Social media became the most effective source of practical recovery information because it was crowdsourced by people actively solving similar problems. However, social media came at a cognitive cost: sorting through noise, opinions, and misinformation was exhausting and time-consuming. The U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) loan process was particularly difficult because eligibility and requirements were highly individualized and administratively burdensome, requiring about a week of dedicated effort. Crowdsourcing helped, but accuracy remained inconsistent.
column6: The participant’s most pressing current need is financial and tax planning. Recovery has shifted into a more complex financial phase involving tax implications, lawsuit planning, and strategic use of anticipated recovery funds. Professional financial guidance (tax experts, financial planners) is now seen as necessary to manage these downstream complexities.
column7: Technology and AI were deeply integrated into recovery. The participant had prior professional experience with AI and used it for practical recovery tasks, including reconstructing lost household inventory by estimating contents of spaces (e.g., “what was likely in an 8x5 closet”), understanding tax implications, and supplementing recovery planning. AI was especially useful for building structured inventory lists when memory was incomplete. The participant also used a home inventory/photo-analysis tool to reconstruct household contents. AI was considered more useful than social media in some contexts because it reduced noise and improved organization. It was also used for lifestyle support (exercise, meditation planning), though not for therapy
column8: The participant expressed high trust in AI and minimal privacy concerns, provided systems maintain enterprise-grade safeguards (e.g., SOC 2 compliance). They emphasized the importance of training AI on relevant population-specific data to improve usefulness. They recognized additional complexity for international data (e.g., European privacy standards). AI was viewed as highly practical and valuable for structured recovery tasks, less so for emotionally nuanced or bureaucratically complex systems like SBA applications.
column9: relevance beats volume. Survivors don’t need “more information”; they need situationally precise information filtered for their exact recovery profile. This interview strongly supports adaptive routing logic

My advice to people would be to find friends or family that can activate during a crisis and help. For impacted families there is no time for anything but survival. By the time friends asked if they could help we were already steps ahead so couldn't benefit. Some of the things the friend/family member could do:
 1. start looking for rental units...the sooner you find a place the sooner you avoid price gouging and location constraints.
 2. start a go fund me. We would never have thought of this, and the sooner it is up the more folk will support. It is human nature to move on quickly, so people will start to turn their attention away within a couple weeks of the disaster.
 3. Find anchors to normalcy. It's a disaster but not a shared one. The vast majority of the planet is still normal. It's important to be reminded what that looks like.
 

 This would need to be done ahead of time, and ideally the friend would be given details that would be helpful when they operate on their behalf.

column3: Recovery appears to have involved major family restructuring, educational disruption for children, and prolonged insurance-related administrative burden. Re-establishing routines and creating stability for children emerged as a major practical focus.  School burned down and home burned down.  Had trouble finding a new school that would take them.  Ended up going to their old school that relocated in an office building to provide kids with continuity with teachers and friends.
column4: The participant relied heavily on cognitive reframing to cope—focusing on what was still intact (family safety) rather than only on losses. They allowed space for emotional breakdown (“cry fest”) but emphasized recalibrating perspective and continuing forward. A major turning point was debris removal and lot clearing; until then, uncertainty stalled progress. Once the lot was cleared, the participant regained a sense of agency and control over the recovery process. For the children, restoring routine and familiar structure (school, possessions, personal space) was central to emotional adjustment. Community donations accelerated this stabilization. Sending the children to Canada temporarily to reconnect with extended family and normalcy provided additional emotional buffering, especially given the family lacked local relatives in the U.S.  Have operation "one christmas" to get back in their rebuild home before the next holiday is very motivating.
column5: Two major pain points emerged: (1) school placement and educational continuity, and (2) insurance. Schooling was highly stressful because executive orders expanded access, but finding the right fit for children—especially those with needs like Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)—was difficult. Some schools were poor fits or delayed placement, creating instability and forcing strategic navigation of the system. Maintaining continuity with their original school, even in a temporary office-building setup, became the best available option. Insurance was described as deeply inhumane, adversarial, and exhausting. The participant described repeated delays, denials, and bureaucratic barriers, particularly with State Farm, while observing that other survivors received faster payments from different insurers. The inequity of insurer responses compounded frustration and distress.

column7: Technology and AI were used extensively for practical recovery tasks. The participant’s spouse, who works in AI, built scripts and prompts to reconstruct household inventories by pulling purchase histories from Amazon and estimating replacement costs. AI was used to generate inventory documentation for insurance claims, reconstruct household contents, and support home redesign decisions by comparing old and new house plans. AI functioned as an efficiency tool for administrative and financial recovery tasks.
column8: The participant experimented with ChatGPT for emotional support/coaching but found it overly affirming and insufficiently critical or practical. The feedback felt “too nice” and lacked the level of realism or challenge they needed. This suggests a preference for more grounded, direct, and strategically useful coaching rather than generic positivity.

column3: Nearly one year post-fire, recovery remained deeply intertwined with ongoing personal, family, and work stressors, creating chronic overwhelm and a persistent sense of “not enough hours in the day.” The participant described stress around known deadlines and anxiety about unknown deadlines they might be missing. The insurance claim remained open, requiring a detailed inventory process to recover the remaining 25% of personal property coverage. Reconstructing inventory was emotionally difficult because each item carried memories. Pandemic-era online shopping records (e.g., from Amazon) helped reconstruct losses. Additional caregiving burden compounded recovery: the participant was living in a relative’s townhouse while managing that relative’s declining cognition related to Dementia and taking over financial/property affairs, including unresolved tax issues. Early in the disaster, the participant experienced basic self-neglect (e.g., forgetting to eat) because the recovery process felt so overwhelming and undefined. The first phase was dominated by logistics—turning off utilities, stabilizing housing, and figuring out where to start. Professional disruption was buffered by temporary workplace closure at Jet Propulsion Laboratory, allowing space to focus on recovery. Social support was strongest when people acted concretely (bringing food, supplies, money) rather than offering vague help. Prior experience with the Lahaina wildfire shaped the participant’s evacuation decisions and heightened situational awareness.
column4: Emotional processing was largely displaced by logistical focus. The participant used task lists and checking off completed items as a way to maintain momentum and reduce overwhelm. There was little space for emotional reflection during acute recovery. The participant described wanting “home” but having nowhere to return to, highlighting the emotional dislocation of total loss.
column5: The participant stayed connected to multiple survivor and neighborhood groups (including Facebook communities with survivors from the Camp Fire) to track opportunities, updates, and aid. Fear of legal entanglement and administrative burden made the participant avoid lawsuits, even when compensation might be available. Observing long-term unresolved litigation (e.g., against Pacific Gas and Electric Company) reinforced that avoidance. A major source of stress was changing tax law: previous tax protections on disaster settlements had expired, creating anxiety that any future settlement could be heavily taxed and financially undermined. Bureaucratic complexity itself became a major source of distress.
column6: Over time, the participant reported a major shift in values and emotional priorities. Material possessions lost emotional significance, and tolerance for everyday inconveniences increased (“care meter” is lower). Travel and life disruptions no longer felt as upsetting. Clothing and possessions became utilitarian rather than emotionally meaningful. This reflects an adaptation toward detachment from material identity and reduced emotional investment in tangible things.
column7: The participant downloaded an AI-based mental health app (possibly Sunny) for stress management but did not engage with it consistently. They also participated in workplace trauma talks and educational sessions from trauma and PTSD experts, which helped normalize reactions. The participant noted that many automatic routines and habits disappeared after the fire, highlighting functional disruption.
column8: The participant found AI appealing because it reduced fear of judgment and increased willingness to disclose honestly compared to talking with a human. A key desired function for AI was reassurance and validation—confirming whether they were “doing the right thing” in the recovery process. Timing and emotional state mattered; support needs varied depending on mood and emotional volatility. The participant emphasized that during acute recovery, logistical support mattered more than emotional processing. In-person disaster recovery centers were described as extremely helpful because they consolidated practical resources (e.g., Social Security, DMV, aid organizations like CORE Response and United Policyholders) in one place. AI was viewed with some skepticism due to concerns about hallucinations and misinformation. Human oversight and visible safety guardrails were considered essential, especially when users are vulnerable.

column3: The participant experienced compounding crises layered on top of the wildfire: caregiving collapse, spousal medical decline, displacement, and later job loss. Prior to the fire, the participant was already the sole caregiver for a wife with progressive cognitive decline and had reached caregiving limits, beginning to explore memory care. The fire accelerated everything. Multiple evacuations destabilized the spouse significantly, leading to acute decompensation, hospitalization, inability to walk or talk, refusal to eat, and eventual transition into a memory care facility—first in Culver City and later another facility farther away. This created cascading disruptions in caregiving routines and family structure. Their twin sons (age 18, both on pause from college) were also affected. The participant’s role shifted from in-home caregiver to navigating healthcare systems, memory care transitions, and repeated hospitalizations while also dealing with disaster recovery. The cumulative burden radically altered daily life.
column4: Temporary stabilization came through concrete support—receiving a donated RV, securing a rental, and having reliable transportation created immediate relief and practical security. Despite this, the participant reported chronic exhaustion and needing excessive sleep (10+ hours), suggesting prolonged physiological stress and depletion even in the absence of overt physical illness. Emotional recovery appears intertwined with physical fatigue and cumulative caregiver burden.
column5: A major non-fire-related but overlapping stressor was job loss from Jet Propulsion Laboratory after 17 years, tied to broader funding and political instability. This represented a major identity rupture: it was the first time in the participant’s life being involuntarily laid off. Retirement planning had been approaching naturally, but the involuntary timing and context made the transition emotionally painful. Financially, the participant felt relatively stable due to retirement planning and Social Security Administration timing, but psychologically it was a major loss of agency and professional identity.
column6: The participant described needing intellectual continuity and unfinished professional work as a stabilizing force. Completing pending scientific papers and abstracts became an important source of meaning, identity preservation, and engagement after job loss. Beyond that, there was recognition of needing to manage ongoing paperwork, deadlines, and eventually rebuild a broader life beyond caregiving and recovery. The phrase “eventually I need to get a life” suggests awareness of long-term identity reconstruction needs.
column7: Continued access to workplace-affiliated disaster recovery support groups through Jet Propulsion Laboratory was important, even after job loss. The participant retained remote access to support systems but lost physical access to the workplace community, which likely reduced in-person social support. Community communication also occurred through WhatsApp neighborhood groups.
column8: The participant expressed skepticism toward AI, positioning that skepticism as potentially useful for critical engagement. The primary concern was the absence of human warmth. While open to support tools, the participant emphasized that medium-term needs likely pointed toward human therapy rather than AI support. Prior experiences with therapy across different life stages (including couples therapy) shaped this perspective, suggesting familiarity with human-based support and its limits.
column9: disaster rarely arrives alone. Recovery is often layered onto pre-existing caregiving, illness, career transitions, and family strain. Intake systems need to assess “stacked burdens,” not treat the fire as the only problem.

column3: The participant described having “no routine” after the fire, with profound disruption to sleep, cognition, and day-to-day functioning. In the immediate aftermath, they felt unable to think clearly, make judgments, or maintain basic routines, including sleep (sometimes awake until 7:30 a.m.). A weekly walking group became one of the only stabilizing routines. The participant described the fire as a deeply transformative, almost existential event—breaking down emotional walls and creating a sense of collective vulnerability and openness within the community. Social connectedness shifted: everyone was affected, reducing the need for explanation or emotional labor. Community leaders (block captains, grassroots organizers) became vital supports. In the immediate phase, the participant spent nights in a car, then at a girlfriend’s house, then with friends for several weeks. The car became a symbol of safety (“happy place”). The participant intentionally withdrew and avoided conversation, describing being in shock and needing silence. Existing asthma also prevented returning to the property.
column4: The participant had longstanding anxiety and depression predating the fire and described the fire as layering onto an already fragile emotional baseline. They reported persistent intrusive imagery (e.g., cars crashing into them), intense longing for home, and a desire for nurturing or maternal comfort. Crying was framed as an adaptive coping mechanism—an emotional release that reduced anxiety. The participant strongly preferred not to talk during the acute phase, lacking bandwidth for emotional processing or responding to family concern. Over time, some comfort with social interaction returned. Anticipatory grief remained intense around inventorying losses, especially artwork and emotionally significant belongings, which the participant expected would trigger deep depressive episodes. Financial loss compounded grief, including the loss of income from an art studio and home rental.
column5: The participant’s biggest pain points centered on financial management and administrative burden. They explicitly identified needing money and someone to organize it (e.g., a bookkeeper). Disaster aid systems (U.S. Small Business Administration loans, California Mortgage Relief Program / CalAssist, unemployment) were confusing, repetitive, and difficult to navigate—especially when uploading documents or understanding what was required. Bureaucratic paperwork was overwhelming, and digital systems felt difficult to manage. Fraud concerns and administrative deadlines created additional pressure. The participant also highlighted sleep disruption as a major barrier to functioning, noting that medications like Lunesta improved sleep but impaired cognition the next day. They were also prescribed Xanax, which they rationed carefully. Better sleep and cognitive clarity were seen as essential recovery supports.
column6: Loneliness emerged as a major long-term challenge. The participant described adapting to solitude but recognizing that connection is the antidote. They maintained a few close friendships where communication felt manageable, but lost some friendships due to reduced capacity for phone conversations. They were also managing an unequal caregiving dynamic with a friend experiencing Dementia, adding relational burden. Over time, the need shifted toward social connection, emotional companionship, and maintaining meaningful relationships without overwhelm.
column7: The participant actively used ChatGPT as a first-stop tool for practical questions—often before using search engines. AI was used for troubleshooting, organizing bills, contractor communication, credit management, and attempting to reconstruct purchase histories from Amazon for reimbursement purposes. The participant relied heavily on digital systems for managing recovery logistics, payments, and rebuilding tasks.
column8: The participant expressed a strong desire for a single, centralized recovery system rather than fragmented paper handouts and multiple disconnected agencies (e.g., Federal Emergency Management Agency, DMV, property tax offices, contractor guilds, charities). They wanted a unified source of information that clearly explained what each resource does and when to use it. Cognitive overload and memory issues made organizing and retaining recovery information especially difficult. The participant also expressed a desire for practical support in locating healthcare providers (dentists, psychiatrists). They emphasized the value of physical presence and embodied support—not just digital information—suggesting that AI should complement, not replace, human contact.
column9: cognitive overload is not just overwhelm—it can look like functional impairment. This participant repeatedly describes memory issues, confusion, and inability to organize information.

column3: Day-to-day work routines returned relatively quickly, with the participant back in person at work, but recovery became a second shift layered onto evenings—coordinating logistics, insurance, and rebuilding tasks with a partner. Existing hobbies (weekly trivia, pottery, creative work) became important anchors of continuity and identity. Housing displacement created major lifestyle changes: temporary housing with friends in Pasadena followed by a rental ADU near work and Altadena. The downsizing and environmental mismatch (limited space, no yard for an aging dog, unfamiliar neighborhood) created additional stress. The first weeks were marked by a “firehose” of information—rapidly changing rules, regulations, forms, and procedural requirements. Social media and community groups became essential for real-time updates, but monitoring and synthesizing that information became a full-time cognitive burden. Learning from neighbors who were slightly ahead in the process helped reduce uncertainty.
column4: The emotional impact was compounded by broader societal instability (economic uncertainty, political shifts, job insecurity), making the disaster feel embedded in a larger atmosphere of instability. Recovery felt omnipresent and impossible to compartmentalize. A major stressor was uncertainty about long-term decisions: whether to stay, move, rebuild, or prepare for employment instability. Avoidance and escapism (reading, pottery, TV, video games) became primary coping strategies. Exhaustion served as an internal signal of emotional overload—after work, the participant often lacked energy for basic tasks or social connection. Hope returned when practical progress emerged, particularly around resolving insurance issues and moving into the more creative, future-oriented aspects of rebuilding (architecture, design, imagining the future home).
column5: A major challenge was situational isolation. Even within broad survivor communities, participants felt isolated by the specificity of their own case (e.g., total loss, smoke damage, renter, homeowner), making it hard to find others whose experience closely matched theirs. Workplace-based support groups at Jet Propulsion Laboratory, active Slack communities, nonprofits, and social platforms helped, but the fragmentation remained difficult. Bureaucratic navigation—especially insurance—was one of the hardest practical burdens. Each policy, lender, and insurer created a different pathway, making peer comparisons both helpful and confusing. Resources like United Policyholders meetings and community groups on Discord and Facebook were helpful but duplicative and scattered across multiple channels. The participant strongly wanted tailored guides (e.g., county-specific, fire-specific, insurance-specific) rather than generic advice. The most helpful support came from a former coworker who had lived through a similar disaster in Colorado. That coworker provided personalized, experience-based support (answering specific questions, checking in on anniversaries, offering practical support like meals) which was more valuable than generic support.
column6: Early needs centered on managing uncertainty and deciding what to do next; because the future was unclear, many decisions were delayed. Now that rebuilding plans are finalized, needs have shifted toward concrete logistics and implementation. However, the participant worries that focusing too much on logistics may crowd out emotional and physical self-care. Community support has remained steady in information-sharing but fluctuates in emotional attunement, as different survivors move through different stages of recovery.
column7: The participant relied heavily on crowdsourced information from multiple digital communities but struggled to remember where information was found because it was scattered across too many channels. They avoided government websites and trusted peer networks more. The participant tried productivity or organizational apps but found none that fit the complexity of disaster recovery. They described being stuck between digital and analog systems (apps vs journals) and struggling to maintain consistent routines with either.
column8: The participant was generally cautious about AI, citing ethical concerns, training data issues, hallucinations, and concerns about AI-based therapy. However, they expressed openness to a carefully designed, evidence-based AI tool with expert oversight and psychological validity. The most compelling AI use cases were emotional regulation and tactical support: quick in-the-moment resets between work meetings, reminders to take breaks, emotional check-ins during stressful insurance or rebuilding tasks, and structured reflection tools to help process experiences and prepare for therapy. The participant envisioned AI as a bridge between therapy sessions—an on-demand support layer rather than a replacement. The participant disliked the overly agreeable tone common in many LLMs (“you’re right” style validation) and wanted something more grounded and authentic.
column9: survivors want both tactical and emotional lanes—but they need to be clearly separated. This participant explicitly points to the importance of knowing when they want practical help vs emotional regulation. That distinction may be a core UX requirement.

column33:
One thing that a fellow survivor mentioned to me was going to a group therapy session, and hearing audible gasps when explaining why she was there (fire + other) and the deep intersection and interplay of all the challenges being faced. It feels hard to find support or resources that “get it” outside of fire survivor communities - it feels like the standard avenues of support don’t know how to best help fire survivors specifically, and the most valuable resources are those who have navigated similar experiences. I also recall going to yoga classes and feeling uncomfortable with the casual metaphors and language around fire; there aren’t yoga classes being offered that cater towards or understand our specific trauma, even in neighbouring communities 10 minutes from Altadena. 
 I think having this kind of specific resource for those recovering from fires, created by those with direct experience and understanding, will be incredibly powerful and helpful. 
 

 Ideas: personalized journaling prompts or reflection questions related to fire recovery; encouragement that is grounded in research and evidence and acknowledges the difficulties without “toxic positivity” or platitudes
